# sidekick

Small, on-device models for the background work beside a bigger one:
session titles, tags, embeddings, classification, reranking. sidekick runs
them on the parts of a Mac a local LLM or an editor leaves idle (the Neural
Engine for encoders, Apple's Foundation Models for short constrained
generation), so they don't compete with the GPU. On Intel Macs and Linux
the same API serves embedders on the CPU through ONNX Runtime.

Compare every model's fidelity and benchmark scores by chip and path:
[ironblock.github.io/sidekick](https://ironblock.github.io/sidekick/).

The daemon, `sidekickd`, speaks the OpenAI API, plus the vLLM and Cohere
shapes for routes OpenAI doesn't have. Anything that takes an
OpenAI-compatible base URL can use it.

| Route | What it serves |
|---|---|
| `POST /v1/chat/completions` | Apple Foundation Models: Apple silicon, macOS 26+, Apple Intelligence on |
| `POST /v1/embeddings`, `/v2/embed` | Embedders, on the Neural Engine, GPU or CPU (Core ML) or the CPU (ONNX Runtime) |
| `POST /v1/classify` | Classifiers, including zero-shot and NLI (Core ML, macOS) |
| `POST /v1/rerank`, `/rerank`, `/v2/rerank` | Cross-encoder rerankers (Core ML, macOS) |
| `POST /tokenize`, `/detokenize` | A model's own tokenizer: count tokens, check an input fits |
| `GET /v1/models`, `GET /health` | What this machine serves, and why anything is unavailable |

The full contract of every route is in [docs/API.md](docs/API.md).

## Who it's for

- **Tools that run a local LLM on the GPU** and want embeddings, labels or
  titles without taking GPU time from it.
- **Apps that want on-device embeddings or classification when available,**
  without a hard dependency: probe the daemon, fall back to an in-process
  library or to nothing ([docs/INTEGRATING.md](docs/INTEGRATING.md)).
- **Anyone who wants to know how faithful a model is on each chip:** every
  model is graded against its original on every compute path it serves
  ([docs/MODELS.md](docs/MODELS.md),
  [ironblock.github.io/sidekick](https://ironblock.github.io/sidekick/)).

## Platforms

| Platform | Chat | Embeddings | Classify, rerank |
|---|---|---|---|
| macOS 26+, Apple silicon | yes | Core ML (Neural Engine, GPU, CPU), ONNX | yes |
| macOS, Intel | no | Core ML (GPU, CPU), ONNX | yes |
| Linux x86-64 and arm64 | no | ONNX | no |

Each has a release archive. Minimum OS versions, the bundled ONNX Runtime
and building from source are in [docs/INSTALL.md](docs/INSTALL.md).

## Quickstart

On an Apple silicon Mac. Pick the latest version on the
[Releases page](https://github.com/ironblock/sidekick/releases); other
platforms' archive names are in [docs/INSTALL.md](docs/INSTALL.md).

**1. Install.**

```sh
VERSION=v0.16.0
NAME=sidekick-$VERSION-aarch64-apple-darwin
curl -LO https://github.com/ironblock/sidekick/releases/download/$VERSION/$NAME.tar.gz
curl -LO https://github.com/ironblock/sidekick/releases/download/$VERSION/$NAME.tar.gz.sha256
shasum -a 256 -c $NAME.tar.gz.sha256
tar -xzf $NAME.tar.gz && cd $NAME
```

**2. Get a model.** `sidekickd fetch` downloads one of sidekick's graded
builds from Hugging Face, checks every file against the checksums built
into sidekickd, and installs it in the models directory:

```sh
./sidekickd fetch bge-small-en-v1.5
```

Fetch installs the builds sidekick has published, listed in
[docs/MODELS.md](docs/MODELS.md#published-builds); every other model is
installed by converting it. Some builds ask you to accept terms first;
fetch shows them and tells you how. Every way to install a model is in
[docs/RUNNING.md](docs/RUNNING.md#installing-models).

**3. Start the daemon.** It reads the models directory when it starts, so
start it, or restart it, after installing a model:

```sh
./sidekickd
```

It listens on `127.0.0.1:8790`. To keep it running across logins, install
it as a LaunchAgent ([docs/INSTALL.md](docs/INSTALL.md#running-as-a-service)).

**4. Embed.** In another terminal:

```sh
curl -s localhost:8790/v1/embeddings -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model": "bge-small-en-v1.5", "input": ["How do I reset my password?"]}'
```

Core ML compiles a model for this Mac before serving it: fetch compiles it
when it installs it, and the daemon compiles anything not yet compiled (after
a macOS update, say) in the background when it starts. A request whose
bucket is still compiling waits for it; the rest take milliseconds.

**5. Chat** (needs Apple Intelligence turned on):

```sh
curl -s localhost:8790/v1/chat/completions -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "apple-fm",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a five-word title for: fixing the flaky login test"}]
}'
```

`curl -s localhost:8790/health` says what's available and why anything
isn't: a missing capability is a 503 with the reason, never a hang.

### From an OpenAI client

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8790/v1", api_key="unused")
vectors = client.embeddings.create(model="bge-small-en-v1.5", input=["hello"])
```

The key is ignored unless the daemon is configured with one
([docs/CONFIG.md](docs/CONFIG.md)).

## Models

Compare every model's fidelity and benchmark scores by chip and path:
[ironblock.github.io/sidekick](https://ironblock.github.io/sidekick/).

sidekick serves embedders, classifiers (sentiment, zero-shot, NLI) and a
reranker. [docs/MODELS.md](docs/MODELS.md) lists every one, with its
grade on each compute path, its prompts, its licence and its training
data. Some starting points:

| You want | Start with |

| Fast English embeddings | `bge-small-en-v1.5` |
| Multilingual embeddings, smaller vectors on request | `embeddinggemma-300m` |
| Labels you choose per request | `nli-deberta-v3-base` |

# The HTTP API

Every route `sidekickd` serves, the fields each takes, and its limits and
errors. The daemon speaks OpenAI's API, and vLLM's and Cohere's shapes for
routes OpenAI doesn't have, so a client written for one of those works
unchanged; this document gives what sidekick adds or does differently.
Two design documents hold the full contracts of classification
([design/classify.md](design/classify.md)) and reranking
([design/rerank.md](design/rerank.md)).

## Contents

- [Routes](#routes)
- [Authentication](#authentication)
- [Errors](#errors)
- [Provenance headers](#provenance-headers)
- [Chat](#chat)
- [Embeddings](#embeddings)
- [Tokenize](#tokenize)
- [Classification](#classification)
- [Rerank](#rerank)
- [Listing models and health](#listing-models-and-health)

## Routes

| Route | What it serves |
|---|---|
| `POST /v1/chat/completions` | Chat models, by `model`: Apple Foundation Models (`apple-fm`) on Apple silicon, macOS 26+, Apple Intelligence on ([BACKENDS.md](BACKENDS.md#foundation-models)) |
| `POST /v1/embeddings` | Embedders, OpenAI's shape |
| `POST /v2/embed` | The embedders, in Cohere's v2 shape |
| `POST /v1/classify` | Classifiers, including zero-shot and NLI: vLLM's `/classify` (Core ML, macOS) |
| `POST /v1/rerank`, `POST /rerank` | Cross-encoder rerankers: vLLM's (Jina's) shape (Core ML, macOS) |
| `POST /v2/rerank` | The same, in Cohere's v2 shape |
| `POST /tokenize`, `POST /detokenize` | An embedder's or text classifier's tokenizer: vLLM's shape |
| `GET /v1/models` | What this machine serves: each model's task, backend, limits and prompts |
| `GET /health` | Availability per backend, and why anything is unavailable |

The daemon listens on `127.0.0.1:8790` by default ([CONFIG.md](CONFIG.md)).
A request body is at most 2 MiB.

## Authentication

With no `api_key` configured (the default), no route needs a key, and an
OpenAI client may send any. With one
([CONFIG.md](CONFIG.md#the-config-file)), every route except `/health`
needs `Authorization: Bearer <key>`, `/v1/models` included; a missing or
wrong key is a 401 with code `invalid_api_key`. `/health` stays open for
probes, and carries no credentials
([D13](DECISIONS.md#d13--default-bind-1270018790-health-unauthenticated)).

## Errors

Every error, malformed JSON included, is OpenAI's shape:
`{"error": {"message", "type", "code"}}`.

| Status | `code` | When |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | `invalid_request_error` | A field the route rejects, named in the message: an unknown option, an input over the model's limit, or a model sent to a route that doesn't serve its task (the message names the route that does) |
| 400 | `context_length_exceeded`, `content_filter`, `unsupported_language`, `unsupported_schema` | Chat: a prompt over the model's context, a guardrail refusal ([below](#guardrail-refusals)), a language the model doesn't support, or a `response_format` schema guided generation can't use |
| 401 | `invalid_api_key` | A key is configured, and the request's is missing or wrong |
| 404 | `model_not_found` | No model by that id is served |
| 413 | | A body over 2 MiB |
| 429 | `rate_limit_exceeded` | Foundation Models is rate-limiting; `Retry-After` says when to retry |
| 503 | `backend_unavailable` | A backend this machine or build doesn't have, with the reason, which `/health` reports too. Never a hang. |
| 503 | `backend_busy` | Foundation Models is busy; retry |
| 504 | `timeout` | The request's work ran past its model's request timeout ([CONFIG.md](CONFIG.md#per-model-settings)) |
| 504 | `load_timeout` | Its model's or buckets' first load ran past `load_timeout_secs`. `Retry-After` is set: the load continues, so a retry finds it ready |

## Provenance headers

Every inference response carries provenance headers. They follow OpenAI's
`openai-model` / `openai-version` style:
- `sidekick-version`.
- `sidekick-model`: `<id>@<revision>` when the manifest has a `source`,
  otherwise `<id>`. For `apple-fm` it's the Foundation Models variant id,
  read in the background and cached; until it's known, `apple-fm`.
- `sidekick-compute-units`: the configuration the serving instance was
  loaded with: a Core ML model's `compute_units` (`cpu_and_ne` unless its
  manifest says otherwise; see [Compute units](BACKENDS.md#compute-units)), `cpu` for static and ONNX
  models ([D40](DECISIONS.md#d40--an-onnx-runtime-cpu-backend-for-embeddings)).
  `apple-fm` omits it. It reports configuration, not the executing device, which
  Core ML doesn't expose.
- `sidekick-buckets`: the sequence-length bucket each input ran in, in
  input order and comma-separated (`256,256,512`; one input gives `256`).
  ONNX models have no buckets and don't send it.
  Each bucket is its own compiled program ([D15](DECISIONS.md#d15--per-bucket-static-artifacts-pooling-baked-into-the-model)), so this names the
  program that answered each input, the one whose placement `/v1/models`
  reports per bucket (see [Where Core ML places operations](BACKENDS.md#where-core-ml-places-operations)). On
  `/v1/classify`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/rerank`, `/rerank`, `/v2/rerank`
  and `/v2/embed`. A rerank pair is one input, in request order rather
  than the sorted results' order. Chat and static embedders omit it.

## Chat

`POST /v1/chat/completions` serves each chat model `/v1/models` lists with
`task: "text-generation"`; today that is Apple's Foundation Models as
`apple-fm`. A request goes to the model its `model` names, exactly: there
is no default, no alias and no fallback from one model to another. An id
another route serves (an embedder, a classifier) is a 400 naming the route
that serves it; any other id is a 404 `model_not_found`.

Point an OpenAI provider (OpenCode, an editor, a script) at
`http://127.0.0.1:8790/v1` with that model. Constrained output works via
the standard `response_format`; for example, a session title:

```json
{
  "model": "apple-fm",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Title this session: ..."}],
  "response_format": {
    "type":

route's own check, run on the text, under the default
`truncate: NONE`. Use it rather than comparing `count` with
`max_model_len`. The route also refuses a text by its size in bytes (see
above), and some text is far more bytes per token than English. A run
of Thai, Lao, Khmer or Burmese with no spaces can be a single unknown
token to a WordPiece vocabulary, so it fits by count and not by size.
A text of nothing but spaces counts no tokens at all. An empty text
is refused by a Core ML or ONNX model that adds no special tokens.

`count` is the number `/v1/embeddings` compares with the limit. It
includes the special tokens and the prompt prefix, which `input_type`
chooses by `/v1/embeddings`' names or `/v2/embed`'s (`query` or
`search_query`; `document`, the default, `passage` or `search_document`;
or `none`, no prompt), or `prompt_name` chooses by name.
The text is never truncated, so a text over the limit is counted in full.
`max_model_len` is that limit: the model's `max_seq_len` from
`/v1/models`, or lower when the model's own `tokenizer.json` truncates
sooner ([D44](DECISIONS.md#d44--tokenize-and-detokenize-count-as-the-embedding-path-does)). `max_tokens`, `/v2/embed`'s, makes `fits` measure against
it instead, as `/v2/embed` with `truncate: "NONE"` does.
At most 4 MiB of text is tokenized at once, across requests; a request
waits for room within the request timeout.
`add_special_tokens: false` leaves the special tokens out of `count` and
`tokens` (not out of `fits`), and `return_token_strs: true` adds each
token's vocabulary entry as `token_strs`. `/detokenize` takes `{model,
tokens}` and returns `{prompt}`, special tokens kept.

For a text-classification model, `count` and `fits` are `/v1/classify`'s,
without `truncate_prompt_tokens`, which refuses a text over 16 bytes per
token of the limit by its size. Rerankers and zero-shot models are a 400:
their inputs are pairs, or a text laid out with the request's labels, not
one text on its own. So is `messages`, vLLM's chat form, since these
models have no chat template. The chat model is a 400 too, because
Foundation Models reports token counts but not token ids. The routes
aren't mounted under `/v1/`, as in vLLM and SGLang ([D44](DECISIONS.md#d44--tokenize-and-detokenize-count-as-the-embedding-path-does)).

## Classification

`POST /v1/classify` is vLLM's `/classify` (and SGLang's `/v1/classify`),
field for field, so vLLM and SGLang clients work unchanged:

```sh
curl -s localhost:8790/v1/classify -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "nlptown-sentiment",
  "input": ["The battery lasts for days.", "It broke on day two."]
}'
```

The response (values illustrative):

```json
{"id": "classify-…", "object": "list", "created": 1790663954, "model": "nlptown-sentiment",
 "data": [{"index": 0, "label": "5 stars", "probs": [0.01, 0.01, 0.04, 0.22, 0.72], "num_classes": 5},
          {"index": 1, "label": "1 star", "probs": [0.81, 0.14, 0.03, 0.01, 0.01], "num_classes": 5}],
 "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 19, "completion_tokens": 0, "total_tokens": 19}}
```

`probs` follows the model's label order. vLLM's `use_activation: false`
returns raw logits, and `truncate_prompt_tokens` (with `truncation_side`)
truncates. Without it, an input longer than the model's maximum is a 400,
as in vLLM. Every request field vLLM defines is honored or rejected with a
400, never silently dropped.

Zero-shot models take their labels per request, as `candidate_labels`
(Hugging Face's name). laya, the first zero-shot model, also needs a
`question_type`: `choice`, `score` (ordered levels) or `noul` (does a
statement hold: labels `false`, `true`). `probs` then follows
`candidate_labels`:

```json
{"model": "laya-en", "input": "Please reset my password, I can't log in.",
 "question_type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this ticket?",
 "candidate_labels": ["billing: invoices and refunds", "account: login and passwords", "other"]}
```

NLI cross-encoders (`nli-deberta-v3-*`, `roberta-large-mnli`, the
zeroshot-v2.0 models) put each label into a hypothesis and score it as
Hugging Face's zero-shot pipeline does. That score reduces the model's
classes to one number, so a claim the text contradicts and one it never
mentions can look alike. `nli_probs: true` adds each label's
probabilities over the model's own classes:

```json
{"model": "nli-deberta-v3-base", "input": "The config sets port 8080 and enables TLS.",
 "candidate_labels": ["the port is 9090", "the server logs to a file"],
 "hypothesis_template": "{}.", "nli_probs": true}
```

Measured on nli-deberta-v3-base: `probs` is `[0.55, 0.45]`, which
can't tell the two labels apart, but `nli_probs` can:

```json
"nli_probs": [{"contradiction": 0.9999, "entailment": 0.0000, "neutral": 0.0001},
              {"contradiction": 0.0010, "entailment": 0.0001, "neutral": 0.9990}]
```

One object per label, beside the unchanged `probs`. The three-way (MNLI)
models report `entailment`, `neutral` and `contradiction`. The two-way
zeroshot-v2.0 models report `entailment` and `not_entailment`, so they
can't separate contradicted from unmentioned (deberta-v3-base-zeroshot-v2.0-c
gives both labels not_entailment 0.9996). `/v1/models` lists each one's
`nli_classes`. `nli_probs`, and a manifest that names the model's
classes, need sidekickd 0.15.0 or later: an older daemon skips such a
manifest.

`calibration: "model"` applies the temperature the model declares for the
question type and label count; `/v1/models` lists each classifier's
temperatures, labels or `max_labels`, `max_batch`, and the extension fields
it accepts. The full contract is in
[design/classify.md](design/classify.md).

# Backends

What runs each kind of model, and the limits of each. A model's manifest
names its backend (`backend = "coreml"`, the default for an embedder,
`"onnx"` or `"static"`); classifiers and rerankers are Core ML models;
chat is Apple's Foundation Models.

| Backend | Serves | Where |
|---|---|---|
| [Core ML](#core-ml) | embedders, classifiers, rerankers | macOS: the Neural Engine, GPU or CPU on Apple silicon; the GPU or CPU on Intel |
| [ONNX Runtime](#onnx-runtime-on-the-cpu) | embedders | the CPU, on macOS and Linux |
| [Static](#the-static-tier) | embedders | the CPU, anywhere |
| [Foundation Models](#foundation-models) | chat | Apple silicon, macOS 26+, Apple Intelligence on |

Which platform has which backend is in
[INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md#platforms); each model's grade on each compute
path is in [MODELS.md](MODELS.md).

## Core ML

Each Core ML model is one static-shape compiled program (`.mlmodelc`) per
sequence-length bucket ([D15](DECISIONS.md#d15--per-bucket-static-artifacts-pooling-baked-into-the-model)),
or a chain of programs per bucket for a model too large for one
([D37](DECISIONS.md#d37--chunked-buckets-a-chain-of-programs-under-the-anes-weight-limit)).
An input runs in the smallest bucket that fits it. The first load of each
bucket compiles it for the device; what that costs, and how sidekickd
compiles ahead of requests, is in
[RUNNING.md](RUNNING.md#first-loads-and-the-compile-cache).

### Compute units

A Core ML model loads with `.cpuAndNeuralEngine` unless its manifest asks
otherwise ([D14](DECISIONS.md#d14--compute-units-default-to-cpuandneuralengine)): the ANE keeps background work off the GPU. Some models run
badly there. GLiNER2.5-Decide grades A on the GPU at about 34 ms per input,
but C on the ANE, where a prediction takes about 0.11, 0.34 and 1.28 s at
128, 256 and 512 tokens, because its DeBERTa relative-position rewrite is
slow on the ANE ([MODELS.md](MODELS.md)). Such a model
names its compute units with an optional top-level key, in
`classifier.toml` and in an embedder's `manifest.toml` alike:

| `compute_units` | Core ML | |
|---|---|---|
| `cpu_and_ne` | `.cpuAndNeuralEngine` | the default |
| `cpu_and_gpu` | `.cpuAndGPU` | for a model the ANE runs badly |
| `cpu_only` | `.cpuOnly` | |
| `all` | `.all` | Core ML chooses; for measuring |

- The daemon and `libsidekick.dylib` load the model with it, and every
  bucket shares it. Tests and the parity suite can still load any path
  explicitly (`load_with`).
- `sidekick-compute-units` and the model's `/v1/models` entry
  (`compute_units`) report it. A static embedder reports `cpu`, and setting
  the key on one is a validation error.
- An unknown value fails validation, so the registry skips the manifest
  with the reason (in `/health`'s `skipped_models`) and loads the rest.
- [D27](DECISIONS.md#d27--refuse-multi-shape-core-ml-models-at-load-on-macos-27)'s shape guard runs for every choice: it reads the model description,
  which doesn't depend on compute units, so a multi-shape artifact is
  refused on macOS 27 whatever the manifest asks for.
- The parity suite grades every path regardless. The configured one is the
  path a model is served on, so it is the grade that matters for that
  model.

### The ANE weight cap

Core ML runs an ML program on the ANE only while its weights stay under
about 1 GiB. Past that it runs the whole program elsewhere, with no error
and nothing in the log: measured on an M1 Max under macOS 27.0, a program
with 0.964 GiB of weights ran on the ANE and one with 1.022 GiB didn't, and
coremltools documents a 1 GB Neural Engine limit. A model served on the
ANE (`compute_units` `cpu_and_ne` or `all`) whose compiled weights exceed
`MAX_ANE_PROGRAM_WEIGHT_BYTES` (1 GiB) would look ANE-served and not be,
so the registry skips it, as [D28](DECISIONS.md#d28--classification-post-v1classify-vllms-contract-exactly) skips any bad manifest:
- Each bucket is its own program, and each is checked. The weights are
  the files under the artifact's `weights/` directory (an `.mlmodelc`, or
  `Data/com.apple.CoreML/weights/` in an `.mlpackage`), measured as the
  converters measure them (`tools/sidekick_convert/plan.py`), from file
  metadata, without reading them.
- The reason, in `/health`'s `skipped_models` and in `sk_pool_skipped`,
  names the program (a bucket, or one chunk of a chunked bucket, [D37](DECISIONS.md#d37--chunked-buckets-a-chain-of-programs-under-the-anes-weight-limit)), its
  weights and the fixes: convert it in chunks under the limit (`--chunks
  auto`), serve it on the GPU (`compute_units = "cpu_and_gpu"`), convert a
  quantized variant (`--int8-embedding`), or load it anyway. When the
  daemon config's `[models."<id>"]` chose the ANE ([D38](DECISIONS.md#d38--the-operator-may-choose-a-models-compute-units)), the reason says
  so and names removing that override first.
- Loading it anyway, for experimentation: `ane_weight_limit = "ignore"`
  in the manifest (top level, either manifest file), or `sidekickd
  --ignore-ane-weight-cap` (`ignore_ane_weight_cap = true` in the config)
  for every model.
- Models served on `cpu_and_gpu` or `cpu_only` aren't checked. Neither is
  the parity suite's registry: it measures every compute path itself, and
  its ANE plan check reports a model Core ML doesn't place on the ANE.

### The CPU sequence cap

Core ML's fp16 CPU matmul sums in an order that depends on the contraction
length past 1,024 keys. Each result is accurate within its own rounding,
but a model then gives slightly different answers for the

rs, so that architecture and task
don't multiply into one script per combination:

- **Backbone** (`sidekick_convert.backbones.<family>`): the architecture
  made convertible. It loads the checkpoint in fp32 and applies what that
  architecture needs: the attention implementation and finite masks,
  traceable helpers, position offsets, and the precision and range rewrites.
  It knows how to call the model inside the traced wrapper (`call`), which
  constant buffers the wrapper needs per bucket (`buffers`), and how to run
  the unpadded fp32 reference (`reference`).
- **Head** (`sidekick_convert.heads`): what the artifact returns.
  `pool.Pool` pools an embedding in-graph for Core ML (CLS, mean or last
  token, optionally L2-normalized); an ONNX export leaves that pooling to the
  server. `sequence.SequenceClassification` is the checkpoint's own
  classification head, run through its task class, so each family's head
  semantics are exactly the checkpoint's; a reranker is this head with one
  label and a token_type_ids input. `per_token.PerToken` applies a module to
  every token and returns one value per token, `(1, S)`; the runtime reads
  the positions it placed (GLiNER2's `[L]` label markers).
- **Interface** (`core.Port`, `sidekick_convert.manifest`): the int32
  static-shape inputs, the output name, and the committed manifest the
  artifact must match.

`wrapper.compose(backbone, head, ports)` builds one static wrapper per
bucket; `recipes.embedder()` and `recipes.classifier()` turn the three into
a `core.Job`; `core.run(job, install_dir)` converts and installs it (an
ONNX job goes to `onnx_export.run()` instead, without buckets).

A backbone's contract, for a new family: `model` (the module the wrapper
holds, under the attribute `attr`, which names the converted weights),
`buffers(seq)`, `call(wrapper, inputs)`, `reference(ids, token_type_ids)`,
`example(seq, ports)`, `hidden_size`, `vocab_size`, `config`, and
`forbid_ops`. Rewrites (activation swaps, range and precision rewrites) are
functions of a backbone, applied by the recipe after the fp32 references
are computed from the unmodified checkpoint, so the fp32 gate proves each
rewrite exact.

## The conversion run and its gates

For a Core ML job, for every bucket, `core.run()`:

1. builds the static-shape wrapper, `Job.make_wrapper(seq)`, so a recipe may
   differ per bucket (if one does, bucket invariance across the boundary
   still has to hold);
2. runs the **torch gate**: the padded, static-shape, rewritten wrapper must
   reproduce the checkpoint's own unpadded fp32 forward (embedders: cosine
   ≥ 0.99999; classifiers: max |Δlogit| ≤ 1e-3);
3. traces it and converts with coremltools to an ML program (macOS 15 opset,
   int32 inputs with static shapes);
4. refuses the graph if it contains a **forbidden op**: Core ML's fused
   `scaled_dot_product_attention` always (D25), plus whatever native op a
   rewrite replaced (`gelu`, `silu`);
5. compiles it with `xcrun coremlcompiler`, and gates the compiled artifact,
   the exact bytes that get installed:
   - **compute plan** (D24): every linear, matmul and conv on the ANE, at
     least 80% of assigned ops on the ANE, and no fused attention reading a
     mask built outside its ANE procedure (D25). An unreadable plan, or one
     with every op unassigned, fails, after one re-read from an APFS clone
     (see the stale-cache gotcha);
   - **accuracy per compute path**: CPU_AND_NE (what sidekick serves) and
     CPU_ONLY (an independent execution of the same graph). Embedders:
     cosine ≥ 0.999 against the fp32 reference. Classifiers: the served
     decision agrees with fp32 (the argmax wherever the fp32 top-2 margin is
     ≥ 0.05; for a multi-label case, each label's sign wherever its fp32 logit
     is ≥ 0.05 from 0), and max |Δp| after the activation;
   - **pad invariance**: the same input with random pad ids must give the
     same output. It catches a dropped attention mask (D25) and a mixer that
     reads pad states (D19) in seconds;
   - **finite output**;
6. with more than one bucket, re-exports every bucket against one shared
   weights file, gated ([Shared weights across buckets](#shared-weights-across-buckets));
7. installs `model_{seq}.mlmodelc`, hard-linking identical weight files,
   then the tokenizer and manifest. Nothing is installed until every bucket
   has passed every gate.

Every metric is NaN-safe (`metrics.py`): Python's `min(worst, nan)` returns
`worst`, which once hid a NaN-producing CPU path behind "parity 1.000000"
(D25). A negative-control flag turns gate failures into reports. Latency is
measured only with `--time`: it moves with machine load, and accuracy
doesn't, so time only on a quiet machine.

## Techniques

Each module in `sidekick_convert.techniques` states the limit it works
around and where it was measured.

| module | what it handles | when to use it | measured in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `masks` | finite additive masks (`MASK_ADD = -30000`; `finfo.min` is -inf in fp16 and NaNs softmax), bands, causal masks, `self_attending()` so no query row is fully masked | every model; `self_attending` wherever a row can be fully masked (sliding windows, pairwise masks) with a softmax variant or op that NaNs on it | D15, D25 |
| `attention` | `explicit()` matmul → softmax → matmul, never the fused op; `matmul_softmax()` opt-in: the denominator comes from the value matmul, because the ANE's `reduce_sum` is the one op not bit-identical across compiled buckets | `explicit` always (or pass `scale=` to `F.scaled_dot_product_attention`, which makes coremltools emit explicit ops); `matmul_softmax` only as a measured per-model change | D25 |

## Shared weights across buckets

Each Core ML bucket is its own program, and each program (each chunk of a
chunked bucket) reads its constants from `weights/weight.bin`. The weights
are the same in every bucket, but separately converted files aren't:
coremltools writes constants in program order, and the few that depend on
the bucket (folded position and token-type tables, RoPE tables, the causal
mask, all under 1 MB at 512 tokens) shift every tensor after them. So a
model with three buckets stored its weights three times. Since D49 the
converter stores them once per chunk (`shared_weights.py`):

- **The re-export.** After every bucket has passed its gates, the
  converter loads each bucket's saved `.mlpackage` back into MIL and writes
  it again, with no graph passes, against one union weights file per chunk:
  each distinct tensor (by dtype, shape and bytes) is written once, in
  bucket order, so the tensors every bucket holds come first and each
  bucket's own follow. Every bucket's program then points into the same
  file, and is compiled with `xcrun coremlcompiler` as before.
- **Gates.** The union build replaces the separate one only if:
  - every compiled `weights/weight.bin` in the chunk is the union file,
    byte for byte;
  - every compiled `model.mil` equals the separate build's once weight
    offsets are set aside: the same program, with its constants elsewhere;
  - on CPU_ONLY, CPU_AND_GPU and CPU_AND_NE, every program gives the
    separate build's outputs on the gate cases, bit for bit (each chunk fed
    the separate build's input, so each program is judged alone). Each
    comparison runs in a child process with a Core ML cache of its own,
    deleted when it exits, so the check leaves no compiled copies behind.

  A failure stops the conversion; `--no-shared-weights` converts with one
  file per bucket, as before D49.
- **Keeping the packages.** The converter deletes each `.mlpackage` once
  it is compiled. `--keep-packages DIR` (an empty or new directory) keeps
  them: each bucket's package as converted in `DIR/separate/`, and the
  re-exported packages the installed programs were compiled from in
  `DIR/shared/`, their identical weight files hard-linked. Keep them for a
  build you publish: the published files are the compiled programs, and
  the packages let them be recompiled, or compared before compilation.
- **Per chunk, never across chunks.** The ANE's weight limit (D32) is
  judged on the whole weights file a program references, not on the
  tensors it reads: a file spanning both of Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B's chunks
  (about 1.2 GB) put every chunk on the CPU. So chunk k of every bucket
  shares one file, and no file spans chunks. For a model served on the ANE,
  a union file over the limit keeps that chunk's files separate, and the
  converter says so; the union is the shared weights plus every bucket's
  own tables, so it is a little larger than any one bucket's file.
- **Install.** The union files are installed as one file with a hard link
  per bucket. A move within one filesystem keeps the links; after a move
  across filesystems, or a copy that doesn't preserve hard links (`cp -R`),
  `python -m sidekick_convert.shared_weights link <model-dir>` links
  identical weight files again. It keeps a copy wherever the filesystem
  refuses a link. `ditto` and `rsync -aH` preserve hard links; `cp -Rc`
  (APFS clones) saves the disk too, with a separate file per bucket.
- **What is shared:** the files on disk, and so the download (D49 records
  the publishing format). The daemon needs no change: each bucket is still
  its own program at its own path, and the weight-limit check sums each
  program's own files.
- **What isn't:**
  - **Core ML's compile cache** keeps a specialized copy of the weights
    per bucket and per compute path, as it did (for Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B,
    about 3.6 GB on the GPU or CPU for three buckets). On the GPU and the
    CPU that copy is in the loading process's cache under its home; an
    ANE compile leaves only about 12 kB there and its program, about the
    weights' size, in the system's ANE cache (see "Core ML's cache"
    below).
  - **Memory.** Each loaded bucket maps its own copy from that cache, so
    two loaded buckets map the weights twice, as before.
  - **Compile time.** Every bucket is compiled for each compute path on
    its first load, as before.
- **Measured** (M1 Max, macOS 27.0, coremltools 9.0): weight

## Will a new model convert? A checklist

Read the model's `modeling_*.py` before anything else. The recipe survives:

- **Encoder-style, single-vector output** — bidirectional attention (or a
  published bidirectional patch), CLS or mean pooling; or a causal decoder
  with last-token pooling (F2LLM). Multi-vector, and rerank heads don't fit
  the API; generative models have no pooled vector at all.
- **Last-token pooling has two traps** — (1) select the last real token
  in-graph via the mask (`mask · (1 − shift_left(mask))`, masked sum), never
  a data-dependent gather index; (2) the embedding IS the trailing EOS
  token, so truncation must preserve it — the server keeps `[first max-1,
  last]` for exactly this reason. A short-input-only parity gate misses
  both; test an over-length input that fills the largest bucket.
- **Explicit attention with fp16-safe masks.** For Core ML, masks must use a
  finite constant such as -30000, not `-inf`/`finfo.min`, which NaN in fp16
  (D15). The converters patch the mask builders to do this. Then use
  attention that converts to explicit matmul → softmax → matmul (gemma,
  F2LLM, ModernBERT via `attn_implementation="eager"`). Passing `scale=` to
  `F.scaled_dot_product_attention` works too: coremltools then emits
  explicit ops instead of the fused one. Whatever the form, `ane_check`'s
  pad-invariance gate must pass.
- **Fused SDPA drops the mask on the ANE when the mask is an input of the
  ANE procedure that runs the attention.** That is, when no op inside that
  procedure computes the mask. It may be a model input, the output of an op
  on the CPU, or the output of an earlier ANE procedure. The output then
  equals unmasked attention exactly, for every mask shape, dtype and fill
  value tried and at both opsets (D25). The compute plan shows it:
  - `scaled_dot_product_attention` is on the NeuralEngine, and
  - its `attn_mask` comes from a model input or a CPU op, or from an ANE op
    with a CPU op between it and the attention.

  ModernBERT builds its masks before the CPU-only embedding gather, so the
  mask plumbing lands on the CPU. `python tools/repro_sdpa_mask.py --check
  <model>` applies the rule to a compiled model. A fused attention whose plan
  shows no device (bge-small) is correct only through a Core ML fallback that
  doesn't run it natively. At the iOS26 opset that fallback is gone and bge
  fails to load on CPU_AND_NE, so keep the macOS15 target for fused-attention
  models.
- **Fused SDPA on the CPU (`CPU_ONLY`) has two more defects**
  (reproduced by the same tool):
  - A query row whose keys are all masked returns NaN when
    |fill| × √head_dim > 65504, e.g. -30000 at head dim 64. Explicit
    attention returns a finite row.
  - q/k/v split straight off a packed projection with
    `.transpose(3, 1).unbind(2)` give wrong output. `.permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4)`
    is correct.

  CPU_ONLY parity catches both.
- **Static-shape-friendly graph** (for Core ML; an ONNX export takes dynamic
  axes by design) — no data-dependent shapes. Stock
  `rotate_half`/`repeat_kv` and any `F.conv1d(padding=shape-derived)`
  need the traceable rewrites (D17 constraint 8, LFM2.5 constraint B).
- **fp16-safe activations** — calibrate first (forward hooks, max |activation|
  on a mixed corpus). Under ~30k: convert directly (bge, LFM2.5). Over:
  apply the D17 power-of-two range rewrite (gemma). For Core ML, watch for
  `-1e9` mask constants (rewrite at -30000) and rmsnorm eps below ~1e-4.
- **Keep every linear-layer input near rms 1.*

## Repositories and their layout

One repository per model per backend, under the
[`sidekickd`](https://huggingface.co/sidekickd) Hugging Face organization:
`sidekickd/<model id>-coreml` and `sidekickd/<model id>-onnx`
([data/publishing.toml](data/publishing.toml)'s `owner`). The model id is
sidekick's (models.toml), so a client finds the repository from the id it
already uses. Uploads use the maintainer's own token, which needs write
access to the organization.

```
sidekickd/bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0-c-coreml
  README.md              the model card (tools/model_card.py)
  fp16/                  one build: exactly the directory sidekick installs
    classifier.toml        (or manifest.toml)
    tokenizer.json
    model_128.mlmodelc/    one compiled program per bucket
    model_256.mlmodelc/
    ...
  fp16.sha256            every file of fp16/, `shasum -a 256 -c` format
  NOTICE, TERMS.md, ...  where the licence or tier requires them
```

- **Every quantization and variant of a model is a directory** in the same
  repository, named for its variant in the ledger: `fp16/`, `int8/`,
  `fp16-max2048/`. Each is a complete model directory; a user downloads
  one.
- **Buckets and chunks keep their install names**, `model_<len>.mlmodelc`
  and `model_<len>.<chunk>.mlmodelc` (D37), rather than a
  `buckets/<len>/chunk-N` tree: the published tree is the install tree
  (D49), so nothing is renamed between the ledger, the repository and the
  models directory.
- **A shared weights file (D49) is uploaded at every path it occupies.**
  The Hub stores files by content, so one file at three paths should be
  stored once. The first upload checks that (below); if it isn't, the build
  is uploaded with each distinct file once, at its first path, and fetch,
  which already follows the ledger's path list, is unchanged.
- **ONNX repositories hold sidekick's own exports.** Where the model's
  publisher ships an export of its own that grades A, the card lists it as
  an alternative at a pinned revision and sha256
  ([data/publishing.toml](data/publishing.toml)).
- **Builds are never overwritten.** A converter, coremltools or OS change
  that moves a build's checksums is a new ledger entry and a new commit to
  the repository, tagged with the sidekick release that publishes it; the
  old commit stays reachable at its revision, which the old ledger entry
  records.

## The checksum ledger

[data/ledger.json](data/ledger.json) records every build sidekick converts,
published or not, including builds whose licence keeps them off the Hub.
Reconverting a model and comparing it with its entry shows whether a
converter, coremltools, Xcode or macOS change moved it, and which layer.

One entry per build:

| field | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `id` | `<model>/<backend>/<variant>/<digest[:12]>` |
| `model`, `source` | the models.toml id, and `repo@revision` it was converted from |
| `backend`, `variant`, `quantization` | `coreml` or `onnx`; the build's directory name in its repository; `fp32`, `fp16`, `fp16 weights` or `int8` |
| `buckets`, `chunks`, `max_seq_len` | the build's shape, from its programs and manifest |
| `layout` | `shared` when a weights file is held at several paths (D49), else `separate` |
| `digest` | sha256 over every (path, file sha256) pair in path order: the build's identity, however its files are stored |
| `fingerprint` | the build fingerprint tools/mteb_transfer.py records, from the same hashes |
| `produced` | converter and its commit, coremltools, PyTorch, Python, OS, Xcode, machine, conversion date; `null` where nothing recorded it |
| `files` | each distinct file once: sha256, size, and every path that holds it |
| `grades` | the parity reports that graded these exact files: path, chip, OS, letter, report |
| `published` | each upload: repository, revision, date, sidekick release |
| `evidence`, `recorded`, `note` | `hashed` (from the files) or `sha256sums` (from an archived listing); when; anything else |

**Why JSON, not TOML.** The ledger is written by tools, never by hand:
`ledger.py add` and the converters (next) append to it. Python's standard
library reads TOML but can't write it, and the repository's tools are
standard-library only; JSON round-trips exactly, diffs line by line with one
key per line, and is what fetch (Rust, serde) reads most simply.

**Grades by hash.** `ledger.py add --reports DIR` reads parity reports
and attaches the grades of every report that graded this build's files. A
Core ML report records a 12-hex-digit sha256 prefix of each bucket's
weights, and matches when its buckets are exactly this build's with the
same weights; an ONNX report records the full sha256 of the graph, its
external weights files and the tokenizer, and matches when every one is
this build's file at the same path. By default only reports
[data/runs.toml](data/runs.toml) describes count, the ones whose grades are
published; `--any-report` also takes a release candidate's own. So a card
can say which grades belong to the very files it lists, rather than to an
earlier build of the same model.

**Tooling** (`tools/ledger.py`, standard library only):

```sh
python3 tools/ledger.py add <model dir> --reports <reports dir> [--variant fp16-max2048] \
    [--converter-commit SHA --python 3.12.13 --os "macOS 27.0 (26A428)" --xcode "27.1 (27A9275)" \
     --chip "Apple M1 Max" --torch 2.13.0]
python3 tools/ledger.py add --sums <archive>/item.SHA256SUMS --sums-prefix <dir>/ --model ID [--sizes LIST]
python3 tools/ledger.py verify <model dir> [--id BUILD] [--partial]
python3 tools/ledger.py check
python3 tools/ledger.py list [MODEL]
python3 tools/ledger.py published BUILD --repo sidekickd/NAME --revision SHA --sidekick X.Y.Z
```

- `verify` exits non-zero on any difference and names the layer: weights,
  compiled program, compile analytics, graph, tokenizer or manifest, and a

vel, keeping its
  start, until the sequence fits the largest bucket, and the `.` is then
  appended as for any text. The schema is never truncated: a schema that
  doesn't fit on its own is a 400.
  `truncate_prompt_tokens` and `truncation_side: left` are 400s.
- **fev format:** the state is truncated to `state_max_len` tokens,

  `truncate_prompt_tokens` and `truncation_side: left` are 400s.
- **agentjev format:** nothing is truncated, as AgentJev refuses an
  over-long path: a tree longer than the largest bucket is a 400 naming

- **nli format:** as Hugging Face's pipeline does (`only_first`), only
  the text is truncated, on `truncation_side`, until each label's pair
  fits `max_seq_len`, or `truncate_prompt_tokens` when it's lower. The
  hypothesis is never cut: one that leaves no room for the text is a 400.

Other 400s:
- an empty batch, or more inputs than `max_batch`;
- fewer than 2 candidate labels (1 with gliner2's `multi_label: true`,
  and always 1 on the nli format), or more than `max_labels`;
- duplicate labels, including labels identical at the token level after
  laya's option shrinking;
- a laya `noul` question whose labels aren't `false` / `true` in that order,
  optionally with descriptions (`"false: …"`, `"true: …"`);
- with Julia-1's option rendering: a noul question that describes only
  one of `false` and `true`, a label that renders as an empty option, or
  two labels that render alike (`"b"` and `"x: b"`);
- with the fev format: two labels that render alike once control tokens
  are rewritten (`"<|x|>"` and `"<¦x¦>"`), or a label that renders as an
  empty option;
- with the agentjev format: no `instructions`; an empty input or
  instructions (whitespace by Python's `str.isspace`); two labels that give
  the same candidate text (`"x: b"` and `"b"`), or one that gives an empty
  one;
- no `instructions` for a model whose manifest has no default;
- `multi_label: true` on any format but gliner2 and nli;
- a `hypothesis_template` on any format but nli, or one without exactly
  one `{}` or with any other brace;
- `nli_probs: true` on any format but nli, or on an nli model whose
  manifest doesn't name its `classes`;
- `calibration: model` where the model declares no temperature for that
  question type and label count;
- malformed JSON, on every route, in the API's usual error shape (D22
  amendment).

Where sidekick deliberately differs from vLLM:
- `model` is required. vLLM and SGLang serve one model per process, so
  they can default it; sidekick serves several.
- `truncate_prompt_tokens` keeps the special tokens (`[CLS]`, `[SEP]`) and
  truncates the text between them, on either side. vLLM slices the token
  list including them, so its `left` drops `[CLS]` and its `right` drops
  `[SEP]`, a sequence the model never saw in training.
- Before tokenizing, an input over `max_seq_len × 16` bytes is a 400, or,
  with truncation, is cut to that many bytes first. This bounds the
  tokenizer's work. vLLM has a similar characters-per-token check.
- `calibration: model` is a 400 when the manifest has no temperature for
  the request's question type and label count. laya's own API falls back
  to a per-type temperature there; sidekick declares only what laya fitted,
  and fails loudly otherwise.

## Response

```json
{"id": "classify-<uuid>", "object": "list", "created": 1745383065, "model": "<id>",
 "data": [{"index": 0, "label": "<argmax label>", "probs": [..], "num_classes": 5}],
 "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 10, "total_tokens": 10, "completion_tokens": 0}}
```

- `probs` follows the label order: the manifest's `labels` for fixed-label
  models, the request's `candidate_labels` for zero-shot models. `label` is
  the argmax.
- The activation follows transformers' text-classification pipeline:
  regression → none; multi-label or a single output → sigmoid; otherwise
  softmax, with temperature 1 unless `calibration: model`. On a
  gliner2-format model, `multi_label: true` makes the request multi-label;
  on any other model it is a 400.
- For gliner2 these are the probabilities its own API reports at its
  default activation and temperature 1: a softmax over the task's label
  logits for a single-label task, and each label's sigmoid for a
  multi-label one. (Its per-label training loss is binary cross-entropy,
  but its single-label confidence is the softmax.)
- A multi-label request still returns one `label`, the argmax, because
  vLLM's response shape has one label per input. Clients choose the
  labels that apply by thresholding `probs`. gliner2's own API returns
  every label at or above its `cls_threshold` (0.4 to 0.5 in its
  examples), falling back to the argmax so the answer is never empty.
- `usage.prompt_tokens` counts the real tokens of every input.
- An nli request with `nli_probs: true` adds one field to each result,
  `nli_probs`: per candidate label, in `probs` order, an object of the
  model's classes and their probabilities (see [The nli
  format](#the-nli-format)). Without it, the result has vLLM's four fields
  and nothing else.

`sidekick-model`, `sidekick-compute-units` and `sidekick-buckets`

## The agentjev format

AgentJev (aimeigaoshou/agent-jev; code at malevrigns/agent-jev,
Apache-2.0) is a Qwen3-0.6B decision model with a candidate head. Its
service scores each candidate on its own causal path,

```text
[STATE] state \n[QUESTION] question \n[CANDIDATE] candidate
```

reads the hidden state at the path's last token, and runs a
permutation-equivariant set transformer and a scorer over the candidates'
vectors. Every path of a question shares the state and question, so
sidekick lays the question out once as a tree, and the graph scores every
candidate in one pass. The Rust port of AgentJev's input contract
(`jev_service/contract.py` at the pinned revision: `semantic`, `prepare`'s
candidate rules, `encode_paths`) must copy these exactly:
- Each fragment is tokenized on its own with the model's tokenizer and no
  special tokens, and the ids are concatenated, with no BOS or EOS:
  - the state, as `"[STATE] " + state`, or as sent when it already starts
    with `[STATE]`;
  - the question, as `"\n[QUESTION] " + instructions`;
  - each candidate, as `"\n[CANDIDATE] " + candidate`.
  The tags are plain text, not added tokens. Added tokens in the text are
  matched as the tokenizer matches them, so `<|endoftext|>` in a state is
  that token, as in AgentJev's own service.
- The tokenizer is the checkpoint's `tokenizer.json`, which is
  Qwen3-0.6B-Base's, as AgentJev's service loads. Qwen3-0.6B's (the
  instruct model's) has extra added tokens and isn't interchangeable.
- The state and the instructions must be nonempty once Python's
  whitespace (`str.isspace`, which includes U+001C to U+001F) is
  stripped. Text is otherwise kept as sent.
- Candidates come from the request's labels in label order. A label's
  description is the text after its first `": "`; an empty description
  counts as none:
  - choice: the description, else the label, as AgentJev reads an
    option's value;
  - score: the label as given, as AgentJev reads a level's description;
  - noul: labels `false` then `true`, each optionally described. The
    candidates are the descriptions, else `FALSE` and `TRUE`, AgentJev's
    defaults for undescribed boolean criteria. AgentJev orders boolean
    candidates true first. The head is permutation-equivariant and the
    tree's branches never see each other, so label order changes only the
    order of `probs`.
  Candidates must be nonempty and distinct, as AgentJev requires; either
  failure is a 400.
- The tree is the prefix (the state's and question's ids), then each
  candidate's ids in label order. Per token:
  - `seg`: 0 for the prefix, `c` for candidate `c` (1-based);
  - `position_ids`: `0…P−1` over the prefix, then `P, P+1, …` within each
    candidate, restarting at `P`.
  Each candidate's last token is its `marker_pos` entry. Positions come
  from the layout, never from searching for token ids.
- Nothing is truncated (see "Over-length input"). AgentJev refuses a path
  over 2,048 tokens. sidekick's limit is stricter: the whole tree,
  the prefix plus every candidate, must fit the largest bucket.

The graph's attention lets token `i` attend token `j` when
`attention_mask_j = 1`, `j ≤ i`, `seg_j ≥ 0`, and `seg_j` is 0 or
`seg_i`. A pad (segment −1) attends only itself, so no row is fully
masked and random pad ids change nothing. RoPE reads `position_ids`. Each
candidate therefore sees exactly its own path at its own positions. Against
AgentJev's per-path encoding, through the checkpoint's own head, the tree
reproduced every probability within 2.1e-7 in fp32 (a boolean, a 4-option
choice and a 5-level score). The head reads the hidden state at each
`marker_pos` with one-hot matmuls. It runs the set transformer over the
KMAX slots, with unused slots masked out of its attention and at −1e4 in
the output.

The probabilities are a softmax over the candidates' logits. AgentJev's
service divides the logits by a per-type temperature (`temperatures.json`:
1.0718 for boolean and score, 1.0353 for choice) when it is started with
one, as its card does. sidekick's calibration is opt-in, as on laya:
`calibration: model` applies the manifest's temperatures. AgentJev's are
per type, whatever the candidate count, so the manifest declares each
type's temperature under every one of laya's label-count keys the type can
reach (`noul:2`; `choice:2` … `choice:11+`; `score:2` … `score:6-10`, as
AgentJev takes 2 to 10 levels). A missing bucket would make
`calibration: model` a 400 at that label count. The default is
temperature 1.

Scope, per request:
- **One question.** AgentJev's service takes several questions per state.
  Each is scored on its own paths, so a sidekick request with one question
  is the same computation.
- **String states only.** AgentJev also takes a JSON object or array as a
  state and renders it as compact JSON with sorted keys
  (`separators=(',', ':')`, `ensure_ascii=False`). A sidekick input is a
  string, used as sent: a client reproduces AgentJev's rendering by
  sending that JSON text.
- **`question_type` and `instructions` are required:** the model has no
  default question, and noul labels render differently. `required` in
  `/v1/models` lists `candidate_labels`, `question_type` and
  `instructions`.
- **Labels:** 2 to `max_labels` per request (AgentJev allows 2 to 255
  choices and 2 to 10 levels).
- **The response** is vLLM's: `probs` in label order and the argmax
  `label`. AgentJev's own answers derive from the same distribution: a
  boolean's probability is `p(true)`, and a score's expected level is
  `Σ i·pᵢ`.

## Decisions at a glance

| Area | Decision | Rejected |
|---|---|---|
| Format | A `chat.toml` manifest with `task = "text-generation"` and a versioned program contract: N chunk programs, each one function taking T tokens per call, with its layers' KV cache as Core ML state | A multifunction package with prefill and decode functions (doubles resident weights on the ANE, stalls on every switch); one program (over the 1 GiB limit) |
| Host assets | Embedding table and RoPE tables shipped as fp16 safetensors, mapped, not computed; tokenizer.json; the checkpoint's chat template | An in-program embedding (vocabulary-sized gather, weights on the ANE); RoPE computed at load (libm differences) |
| Compute units | `cpu_and_ne` only; Intel Macs and Macs without an ANE skip the model | `cpu_only` (MLState crash), `all` and `cpu_and_gpu` (ungraded with state) |
| Runtime | Rust, in `sidekick-coreml` (the decoder) and a new platform-neutral `sidekick-llm` crate (the loop) | A Swift shim like `sidekick-fm`'s: an FFI crossing per token, and a second Core ML loader |
| Memory | An autorelease pool around every call; preallocated inputs; output backings if measured equal | Relying on the thread's pool (the spike's loop reached a 19.7 GB footprint) |
| Concurrency | One decoder thread per model, a bounded FIFO queue, one KV state reused across requests | A state per request; batching |
| Tokenizer | The `tokenizers` crate, as the embedders use it | — |
| Template | `minijinja` with Python compatibility, gated against transformers | Hand-written templates per family |
| Sampling | Greedy at temperature 0; temperature and top-p; `seed` honored | Penalties, `n` > 1, `logprobs` (deferred) |
| Structured output | One JSON Schema layer for both backends; llguidance masks each step's logits on the open path | Per-backend schema handling (today's drift: #179, #180) |
| Routing | By the request's `model`, exactly; no fallback between backends | Silent or configured fallback on a guardrail refusal |
| Grading | Teacher-forced top-1 and logit cosine against fp32, anchored on a percentile, with a calibration-stability check; a #174 task slice in the release gate | Grading on the worst position alone (moves with the calibration draw) |

## The model format

### The program contract

A build is N chunk programs over contiguous runs of layers (D37). Every
chunk is a single-function ML program (`main`) with static shapes, called
with T tokens at a time, for the prompt and for generation alike. The
contract is named in the manifest (`interface = "kv-state-1"`), so a later
contract can change it and a daemon that doesn't know it skips the model.

| Name | Shape (dtype) | Chunks | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hidden_in` | `[1, D, 1, T]` (fp16) | all | The residual stream, channels first. For chunk 0 it is the host's embedding lookup; after that, the previous chunk's `hidden_out`, passed without a copy (D37) |
| `pos` | `[1]` (int32) | all | The cache position of the call's first token |
| `mask` | `[1, 1, T, C]` (fp16) | all | Additive causal mask over the whole cache: 0 where key ≤ `pos` + query index, −30,000 elsewhere (finite, D25) |
| `cos`, `sin` | `[T, head_dim]` (fp16) | all | RoPE rows for positions `pos` … `pos` + T − 1 |
| `sel` | `[T]` (fp16) | last | One-hot: which of the T positions' logits to return |
| `hidden_out` | `[1, D, 1, T]` (fp16) | all but last | The residual stream after this chunk's layers |
| `logits` | `[1, V]` (fp16) | last | One row, chosen by `sel`, after the final norm and the head |
| state `k_cache`, `v_cache` | `[layers in chunk, kv_heads, C, head_dim]` (fp16) | all | This chunk's KV cache, written with `slice_update` at `pos` |

**Why one T-token function, T = 16.** #173 found that a multifunction
package shares weights on disk but not on the ANE: loading a prefill and a
decode function doubles the resident weights, and every switch between them
stalls. One function serves both. A call costs only a little more as T
grows, so one function at T = 16 gives a prompt rate about 16 times the
per-token rate, for a modest cost per generated token (#173's third
comment has the measurement). The same width serves speculative
verification and llguidance's forced tokens later at no extra cost. T is a
manifest value, so a later build may choose another.

**Why the cache is static.** The ANE runs static shapes (D15). The cache
capacity C is the attention width every call reads, so a call's cost
depends on C, not on the position (#173). C is judged by D48's cap as a
bucket's length is: a manifest whose C exceeds the model's ANE cap
(`DEFAULT_ANE_MAX_SEQ`, 2,048, or `ane_max_seq_len`) is skipped with the
reason. MiniCPM5-2B's build uses C = 2,048.

**The usable context is C − T + 1.** A call writes T cache positions,
`pos` … `pos` + T − 1, so its first token can sit no later than C − T. The
manifest states the result as `context_length` (2,033 for C = 2,048,
T = 16), and the runtime enforces it.

## Structured output

### One schema layer for both backends

Today each backend reads the request's JSON Schema its own way, and the
Swift bridge's reading is where #179 (unsupported forms answered as an
empty object) and #180 (keys in another order each run) come from: it reads
`type` as a string with `"object"` as the fallback, ignores keywords it
doesn't know, and sorts property names. D8 meant unsupported keywords to
fail loudly; this layer is how they will.

**A schema module in `sidekick-core`** parses `response_format.json_schema`
into an ordered, validated representation of one subset, or refuses it with
a 400 `unsupported_schema` naming the keyword and its JSON pointer. Both
backends consume that representation; neither reads the request's schema
directly.

| Keyword | First release | AFM mapping | Open-model mapping |
|---|---|---|---|
| `type`: `object`, `array`, `string`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean` | yes | `DynamicGenerationSchema` | llguidance |
| `properties`, in the order sent | yes | properties in that order | properties in that order (llguidance's rule) |
| `required` | yes | `isOptional` for the rest | the rest may be omitted |
| `additionalProperties` | absent or `false`; anything else 400 | closed objects | closed objects (`false` set explicitly) |
| `enum` of strings; `const` string | yes | `anyOf` strings | llguidance |
| nullable: `type: [T, "null"]`, or `anyOf` of one schema and `{"type": "null"}` | yes | an optional property; the layer writes `null` where it is absent | llguidance |
| `items`, `minItems`, `maxItems` | yes | `arrayOf` with bounds | llguidance |
| `description`, `title`, `$schema`, `examples`, `default` | accepted; `description` is passed to AFM | a guide | none: the model sees only the prompt |
| `anyOf` (other), `oneOf`, `allOf`, `$ref`/`$defs`, `enum` of non-strings | 400 | — | — |
| `minimum`, `maximum`, `pattern`, `format`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `patternProperties` | 400 | — | — |

The subset is what both backends can honor. A keyword joins it when both
do: llguidance supports the last two rows' keywords (with the coverage its
documentation states), and AFM's generation guides may cover some (number
bounds, a pattern), which is to be confirmed against the SDK and its regex
dialect. Until then a
keyword one backend would honor and the other ignore is a 400 on both,
not a difference in behavior by model. `response_format.json_schema.strict`
is accepted either way; output is always constrained.

**Key order (#180).** The representation keeps `properties` in the order the
request sent them, which needs `serde_json`'s `preserve_order` feature in
the workspace. (llguidance turns it on anyway, by feature unification, so
the workspace enables it explicitly; every `serde_json::Map` the daemon
builds then keeps insertion order instead of sorting, and its JSON outputs
are checked for that.)
- The bridge receives the properties as an ordered list, since a Swift
  dictionary from `JSONSerialization` doesn't keep order, and builds the
  generation schema in that order, so fields are also generated in the
  client's order. The Rust side re-serializes AFM's reply in schema order.
- llguidance generates properties in schema order by construction.
- Both are then byte-identical across runs at temperature 0.

**Optional fields (#177).** The layer keeps JSON Schema's meaning: a
property not in `required` may be left out. It doesn't rewrite optional
properties as required. How AFM's mapping should treat them (#177's
options, such as required-but-nullable) is decided by measurement on the
benchmark's extraction set, and changes only AFM's mapping. On the open
path, the benchmark found llguidance made MiniCPM5-1B fill in fields the
text doesn't state; whether the 2B does is measured before guided
extraction is recommended on it.

### Constrained decoding on the open path

[llguidance](https://github.com/guidance-ai/llguidance) (MIT; Rust; 1.9.1 is
the version the benchmark used) computes, per step, the set of tokens the
grammar allows; the sampler sets every other logit to −∞.
- **API.** One `ParserFactory` per loaded model, built from the tokenizer
  through `toktrie_hf_tokenizers` (which depends on `tokenizers` 0.21 with
  the pure-Rust regex, as the workspace does). Per request, the schema
  layer's representation is written back out as JSON Schema with the
  `x-guidance` options and compiled with
  `TopLevelGrammar::from_json_schema`; a `Matcher` then gives
  `compute_mask`, `consume_token` and `compute_ff_tokens` each step.
  Compiled grammars are cached by the normalized schema's hash.
- **Cost.** llguidance's own figures for a 128k vocabulary are about 50 µs
  of one core per mask typically, about 1.5 ms for a full mask, and under
  30 ms in the worst case it has seen, against a decode step of about
  54 ms (18.6 tokens/s, #173). The mask for the next step depends only on
  the token just sampled, as the next ANE call does, so the two run
  concurrently and the mask is hidden behind the call.
- **Forced tokens are free.** Where the grammar allows exactly one
  continuation (`{"name": "`, a closing brace), `compute_ff_tokens`
  returns it, and those tokens fill the next call's padding slots: a call
  costs about the same for 1 as for 16 tokens. Guided JSON can take fewer
  calls than its token count.
- **Whitespace is bounded** with `x-guidance`'s `whitespace_pattern`, so a
  model can't fill its budget with blank lines inside a valid object. The
  exact bound is measured against llguidance's default on the benchmark's
  extraction and tag sets.
- **`constrained` is true** on every guided open-model reply.

## Transplanting a cache

- **A cache copied to another home, or to another executable's name,**
  hits on the GPU and the CPU, with identical outputs. On the ANE it
  always recompiles. Measured.
- **What an entry holds:**
  - `model.milhash`;
  - `H13C.bundle/H13C.e5`, a manifest with the compiler versions and an
    absolute input path;
  - for the ANE, `main_ane/model.anehash` (129 bytes);
  - for the GPU, a `.mpsgraphpackage` of about 1.0× the weights;
  - for the CPU, a `bnns_program.bnnsir` of about 1.0× the weights.
- **The ANE's program isn't in the home.** There's no `.hwx` there: the
  compiled ANE program lives in the system's ANE cache, kept by Apple's
  `aned` service on the system volume, about 1.0× the weights per compile.
  System Integrity Protection keeps users from removing it, deleting the
  user's cache doesn't free it, and each recompile adds another copy (the
  audit left about 5–8 GB there). Measured.

## Where the compile runs

The ANE compile runs in `ANECompilerService`, a root XPC service, at 94%
of one core and 770 MB resident. `aned` stays at 0%, the loading process
at 2% (splitting the MIL into segments) and the GPU at 0–1%. Measured: the
GPU can't help with the compile.

## Serialization

- Three 6 s ANE compiles took 19.5 s one after another, 19.1 s on threads
  of one process and 18.6 s in separate processes. None overlapped.
- A 2.2 s compile from another process, with another identity, took
  41.9 s: it queued behind a 43 s one.

Measured: ANE compiles are serialized across the whole system. A long
compile delays every app's first ANE load.

## Compile time against length

**bge-small's shape** (attention and MLP): 1.7, 2.7, 3.6, 6.0, 13.8 and
35 s at 128, 256, 512, 1,024, 2,048 and 4,096 tokens. MLP alone compiles
about 15× faster. At 2,048 tokens:

| attention | compile |
|---|---|
| plain (baseline) | 13.8 s |
| fused SDPA | 34.1 s |
| queries in 4 blocks | 26.0 s |
| queries in 16 blocks | 27.2 s |

**Qwen3-Embedding's width at 4,096 tokens, with an attention mask:**

| layers per program | compile |
|---|---|
| 1 | 7.4 s |
| 2 | 16.9 s |
| 4 | 42.6 s |
| 8 | 126 s |

- Compile time is superlinear in the number of layers per program. A
  mask passed as an input costs the same as a constant one.
- With no mask, eight layers compile in 28 s, but predict 2.5× slower.
- Eight one-layer programs compile in about 59 s, against 126 s for one

Measured: the slope comes from masked attention at 4,096 tokens per
program, not from length alone. Splitting a model into more programs (more

class Home:
    """The gate's home: persistent (--home) or temporary (--fresh-home)."""

    def __init__(self, root: Path | None):
        self.temporary = root is None

        self.home = self.root / "home"

        mroot = self.root / "models" / build.model / build.digest[:16]
        dest = mroot / build.model
        text, note = served_manifest(build.dir, build.manifest_name, build.model)
        want = set()
        for rel, src in ledger_tool.walk(build.dir):
            want.add(rel)
            d = dest / rel
            if rel == build.manifest_name and note:
                continue
            d.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            if d.exists() and os.path.samefile(d, src):
                continue
            if d.exists() or d.is_symlink():
                d.unlink()
            try:
                os.link(src, d)
            except OSError as e:
                raise GateError(f"can't hard-link {src} into the gate's home ({e}); put --home on the same "
                                f"volume as the builds")
        if note:
            m = dest / build.manifest_name
            if m.is_file() and m.stat().st_nlink > 1:
                m.unlink()
            if not m.is_file() or m.read_text() != text:
                m.write_text(text)
        for rel, p in ledger_tool.walk(dest):
            if rel not in want:
                p.unlink()
        return mroot, note

    def prune_gpu_cpu(self) -> int:
        """Delete the GPU and CPU programs in Core ML's caches in the home
        (each about the weights' size, recompiled in a second or two), and
        keep every ANE program's. An ANE entry's `<key>.bundle` holds a
        `model.anehash` (under `main/main_ane/`, or under
        `ane_compile/multiprocedure/` for a program split across the ANE and
        the CPU) and stays whole: its CPU segments (`main_bnns`,
        `main_classic_cpu*`) are part of it, and deleting any of it makes the
        ANE compile again. A bundle without one goes. Returns the bytes
        freed."""
        freed = 0
        caches = self.home / "Library" / "Caches"
        for bundle in caches.glob("*/com.apple.e5rt.e5bundlecache/*/*/*.bundle"):
            if not bundle.is_dir() or next(bundle.rglob("*.anehash"), None) is not None:
                continue
            freed += sum(p.stat().st_size for p in bundle.rglob("*") if p.is_file())
            shutil.rmtree(bundle, ignore_errors=True)
        return freed

def free_port() -> int:
    for _ in range(100):
        with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as s:
            s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
            port = s.getsockname()[1]
        if port not in RESERVED_PORTS:
            return port
    raise SystemExit("no free port outside 8790-8799")


def served_manifest(build: Path, manifest_name: str, model: str) -> tuple[str, str | None]:
    """The manifest text to serve, and a note when it differs from the
    build's: an nli manifest without `classes` gains its committed example
    manifest's line (D47), as docs/DECISIONS.md tells an operator to."""
    text = (build / manifest_name).read_text()
    m = tomllib.loads(text)
    nli = m.get("classify", {}).get("nli")
    if nli is None or "classes" in nli:
        return text, None
    example = REPO / "examples" / "classifiers" / model / "classifier.toml"
    classes = tomllib.loads(example.read_text())["classify"]["nli"].get("classes") if example.is_file() else None
    if not classes:
        return text, None
    if len(classes) != nli.get("n_classes"):
        raise GateError(f"{model}: the example manifest's classes {classes} don't match n_classes {nli.get('n_classes')}")
    line = "classes = [" + ", ".join(json.dumps(c) for c in classes) + "]\n"
    patched, n = re.subn(r"(?m)^\[classify\.nli\]\n", lambda mt: mt.group(0) + line, text, count=1)
    if n != 1:
        raise GateError(f"{model}: no [classify.nli] header to add classes under")
    return patched, (f"served with `{line.strip()}` added under [classify.nli], from "
                     f"examples/classifiers/{model}/classifier.toml (D47); the build is unchanged")

# Tag-triggered release: check the release notes, build sidekickd +
# libsidekick.dylib with Xcode 27 (real Foundation Models shim — build.rs
# hard-errors on the stub — compiled against the macOS 27 SDK so the macOS 27
# features are in the binary), prove the daemon still loads on macOS 26,
# build sidekickd for Intel macOS and x86-64 and arm64 Linux, then publish a
# GitHub release
# whose body is the release notes, with every tarball and checksum attached.
#
# Every archive ships the pinned ONNX Runtime (D40) beside sidekickd, as
# libonnxruntime.dylib or .so, with its license: 1.28.3, or 1.23.2 on Intel
# macOS, the last release Microsoft built for it. Each archive is
# smoke-launched twice: with the tiny test ONNX model, the daemon must load
# its pinned runtime from beside it and embed; with no onnx model, it must
# not load the runtime at all.
#
# Each macOS sidekickd is signed ad hoc with a fixed identifier,
# io.github.ironblock.sidekickd (tools/sign_sidekickd.sh), so an upgrade
# keeps Core ML's compiled ANE programs instead of recompiling every bucket.
#
# Release notes are written before tagging, in docs/releases/vX.Y.Z.md, in
# the same change that bumps [workspace.package] version (AGENTS.md):
#
#   git tag -a v0.2.0 -m "sidekick v0.2.0" && git push origin v0.2.0
#
# The tag must match the workspace version and the notes file must exist, or
# the release stops before building.
#
# workflow_dispatch runs the same checks and build as a dry run, for the
# workspace version: artifacts are uploaded to the run for inspection, but no
# release is created.
#
# The xcode-27 runner image is a GitHub public preview (no SLA; jobs may
# queue). Xcode is pinned to a release build because the image also carries
# betas.

name: Release

on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: write

env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always

jobs:
  notes:
    name: Check release notes and version
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.check.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Tag matches the workspace version; notes exist
        id: check
        run: |
          WORKSPACE="v$(sed -n '/^\[workspace.package\]/,/^\[/s/^version = "\(.*\)"/\1/p' Cargo.toml)"
          if [ "${GITHUB_EVENT_NAME}" = "push" ]; then
            VERSION="${GITHUB_REF_NAME}"
            if [ "${VERSION}" != "${WORKSPACE}" ]; then
              echo "::error::tag ${VERSION} doesn't match [workspace.package] version ${WORKSPACE} in Cargo.toml"
              exit 1
            fi
          else
            VERSION="${WORKSPACE}"
          fi
          NOTES="docs/releases/${VERSION}.md"
          if [ ! -s "${NOTES}" ]; then
            echo "::error::no release notes at ${NOTES}; write them before tagging (AGENTS.md)"
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "version=${VERSION}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  build:
    name: Build release artifacts (aarch64-apple-darwin)
    needs: notes
    runs-on: xcode-27
    env:
      DEVELOPER_DIR: /Applications/Xcode_27.0.app/Contents/Developer
    outputs:
      name: ${{ steps.package.outputs.name }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2

      - name: Require the macOS 27 SDK
        run: |
          xcodebuild -version
          SDK="$(xcrun --show-sdk-version)"
          echo "macOS SDK: ${SDK}"
          [ "${SDK%%.*}" -ge 27 ] || { echo "release builds need the macOS 27 SDK, got ${SDK}"; exit 1; }

      - name: Build
        run: |
          # The daemon's honest floor is macOS 26.0 (it hard-links
          # FoundationModels); building for it makes dyld bind every import
          # at launch, which the macOS 26 launch check below relies on.
          # Stripping stays off for this invocation: with a 26.0 deployment
          # target the default debuginfo strip leaves proc-macro dylibs that
          # macOS 27's dyld refuses to load.
          MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=26.0 CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP=none \
            cargo build --release -p sidekick-server --features coreml,onnx --bin sidekickd
          # The C ABI dylib doesn't link FoundationModels; default floor.
          cargo build --release -p sidekick-embed-ffi

      - name: Sign sidekickd with a stable identifier
        # Core ML keys each compiled ANE program to the loading process's
        # code-signing identifier. The linker's is cargo's hashed name
        # (sidekickd-<hash>), which changes with every version, so without
        # this every upgrade recompiles every ANE bucket. Ad hoc, as the
        # linker's signature was. libsidekick.dylib keeps the linker's
        # signature: its identifier is already its file name, and Core ML
        # keys a host's loads to the host process, not to the dylib.
        run: tools/sign_sidekickd.sh target/release/sidekickd

      - name: Verify artifacts are the real thing
        run: |
          # Chat: the FM shim must be linked, not the stub, built with SDK 27.
          otool -L target/release/sidekickd | grep -q FoundationModels
          ./target/release/sidekickd --version | grep -q 'macOS SDK 27'
          vtool -show-build target/release/sidekickd | grep -E 'minos 26\.0'
          otool -l target/release/sidekickd | grep -q LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS
          codesign -dv target/release/sidekickd 2>&1 | grep -qx 'Identifier=io.github.ironblock.sidekickd'
          # C ABI: the exported surface must be present.
          for sym in _sk_abi_version _sk_pool_open _sk_embed _sk_embed_named _sk_model_info; do
            nm -gU target/release/libsidekick.dylib | grep -q " $sym\$"

      - name: Package

A mitochondrion (pl. mitochondria) is an organelle found in the cells of most eukaryotes, such as animals, plants and fungi. Mitochondria have a double membrane structure and use aerobic respiration to generate adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which is used throughout the cell as a source of chemical energy. They were discovered by Albert von Kölliker in 1857 in the voluntary muscles of insects. The term mitochondrion, meaning "a thread-like granule", was coined by Carl Benda in 1898. The mitochondrion is popularly nicknamed the "powerhouse of the cell", a phrase popularized by Philip Siekevitz in a 1957 Scientific American article of the same name.
Mitochondria are commonly between 0.75 and 3 μm2 in cross section, but vary considerably in size and structure. Unless specifically stained, they are not visible. The mitochondrion is composed of compartments that carry out specialized functions. These compartments or regions include the outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane, cristae, and matrix.
In addition to supplying cellular energy, mitochondria are involved in other tasks, such as signaling, cellular differentiation, and cell death, as well as maintaining control of the cell cycle and cell growth. Mitochondrial biogenesis is in turn temporally coordinated with these cellular processes.
Mitochondria are implicated in human disorders and conditions such as mitochondrial diseases, cardiac dysfunction, heart failure, and autism.
The number of mitochondria in a cell varies widely by organism, tissue, and cell type. A mature red blood cell has no mitochondria, whereas a liver cell can have more than 2000.
Although most of a eukaryotic cell's DNA is contained in the cell nucleus, the mitochondrion has its own genome ("mitogenome") that is similar to bacterial genomes. This finding has led to general acceptance of symbiogenesis (endosymbiotic theory) – that free-living prokaryotic ancestors of modern mitochondria permanently fused with eukaryotic cells in the distant past, evolving such that modern animals, plants, fungi, and other eukaryotes respire to generate cellular energy.
